econ-macro-01-c2.text: Dylan G. Rassier (2012). The Role of Profits and Income in the Statistical Discrepancy. Survey of Current Business, U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis.
econ-macro-01-c2.quote: The difference between GDP and GDI is known as the statistical discrepancy. Both GDP and GDI provide a complete picture of economic output, so the statistical discrepancy provides an indication of net measurement error.
econ-macro-01-c2.claim: In practice the three rarely match exactly, because measurement error creates a 'statistical discrepancy'.

econ-macro-01-c3.text: Jonathan D. Church (2016). Comparing the Consumer Price Index with the gross domestic product price index and gross domestic product implicit price deflator. Monthly Labor Review, U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics.
econ-macro-01-c3.quote: but also measures price change for goods and services purchased by businesses, governments, and foreigners.
econ-macro-01-c3.claim: It's broader than CPI because it covers everything in GDP, while CPI covers only consumer goods.

econ-macro-03-c2.text: Michael Bryan. The Great Inflation. Federal Reserve History.
econ-macro-03-c2.quote: A more disruptive force was the repeated energy crises that increased oil costs and sapped U.S. growth.
econ-macro-03-c2.claim: The 1970s oil shocks shifted SRAS leftward, producing higher prices and lower output simultaneously: stagflation.

econ-macro-03-c5.text: Michael Bryan. The Great Inflation. Federal Reserve History.
econ-macro-03-c5.quote: But inflation could also be pushed higher from supply disruptions, notably originating in food and energy markets (Gordon 1975).
econ-macro-03-c5.claim: A negative supply shock (oil crisis) shifts SRAS left.

econ-macro-02-c2.text: Ben S. Bernanke (2003). The Legacy of Milton and Rose Friedman's Free to Choose. Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System (speech).
econ-macro-02-c2.quote: Inflation is always a monetary phenomenon, in the sense that it can be produced only by money growth more rapid than output.
econ-macro-02-c2.claim: Central banks expanding the money supply faster than output grows produces persistent inflation.

econ-macro-02-c3.text: How the Government Measures Unemployment. U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics.
econ-macro-02-c3.quote: People are classified as unemployed if they do not have a job, have actively looked for work in the prior 4 weeks, and are currently available for work.
econ-macro-02-c3.claim: The unemployment rate (BLS U-3) counts only people actively job-hunting.

econ-macro-02-c4.text: Phillips Curve. International Encyclopedia of the Social Sciences, via Encyclopedia.com.
econ-macro-02-c4.quote: In a 1958 article, Phillips plotted annual observations on wage change against unemployment in the United Kingdom for the 1861–1957 period, and he fitted a nonlinear curve by trial and error to the six grouped observations on wage change and unemployment
econ-macro-02-c4.claim: In 1958 A.W. Phillips plotted UK money wage inflation against unemployment over a century and found a strong negative relationship.

econ-macro-04-c2.text: Multiplier. International Encyclopedia of the Social Sciences, via Encyclopedia.com.
econ-macro-04-c2.quote: The Keynesian spending multiplier k, long the workhorse of introductory macroeconomics courses, is 1/(1 – z ), where z is the marginal propensity to spend.
econ-macro-04-c2.claim: The simple Keynesian spending multiplier: 1/(1−MPC), where MPC is the marginal propensity to consume.

econ-macro-04-c5.text: Vanessa Sumo (2008). Jargon Alert: Ricardian Equivalence. Econ Focus, Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond.
econ-macro-04-c5.quote: This is because people understand that whatever amount a government overspends today has to be repaid in the future in the form of higher taxes, thus unraveling a government’s efforts to stimulate the economy.
econ-macro-04-c5.claim: Robert Barro's claim: tax cuts financed by borrowing don't stimulate spending, because rational households know they'll have to pay higher taxes later to service the debt.

econ-macro-05-c1.text: Open Market Operations. Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System.
econ-macro-05-c1.quote: Before the global financial crisis, the Federal Reserve used OMOs to adjust the supply of reserve balances so as to keep the federal funds rate--the interest rate at which depository institutions lend reserve balances to other depository institutions overnight--around the target established by the FOMC.
econ-macro-05-c1.claim: The Fed historically set this rate by buying or selling Treasuries to adjust the supply of bank reserves: open market operations.

econ-macro-05-c3.text: Policy Rules and How Policymakers Use Them. Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System.
econ-macro-05-c3.quote: Policy rules provide useful benchmarks for setting and assessing the stance of monetary policy.
econ-macro-05-c3.claim: It's a benchmark, useful for evaluating policy retrospectively and for guiding judgments about whether current policy is loose or tight.

econ-macro-05-c4.quote: QE involves us buying bonds to push up their prices and bring down long-term interest rates.
econ-macro-05-c4.claim: Quantitative easing (QE): the central bank buys long-dated bonds to push down long rates directly, bypassing the policy rate.

econ-macro-06-c2.text: (1987). Press release: The Prize in Economic Sciences 1987. NobelPrize.org.
econ-macro-06-c2.quote: Solow’s growth model was presented in an article entitled, A Contribution to the Theory of Economic Growth (1956).
econ-macro-06-c2.claim: Robert Solow's 1956 model: output Y comes from labor L, capital K, and technology A.

econ-macro-06-c2.text: (1987). Press release: The Prize in Economic Sciences 1987. NobelPrize.org.
econ-macro-06-c2.quote: An increase in the proportion of incomes which is saved cannot, therefore, lead to a permanent increase in the rate of growth. In contrast, an economy with a higher savings ratio, experiences higher per capita production, and thus higher real income.
econ-macro-06-c2.claim: Higher saving raises the steady-state level of output but not its long-run growth rate.

econ-macro-06-c5.text: (2018). Press release: The Prize in Economic Sciences 2018. NobelPrize.org.
econ-macro-06-c5.quote: Romer’s solution, which was published in 1990, laid the foundation of what is now called endogenous growth theory.
econ-macro-06-c5.claim: The endogenous growth theories of Romer, Lucas, Aghion-Howitt, and others made it part of the model.

econ-macro-06-c5.text: Nicholas Bloom, Charles I. Jones, John Van Reenen, Michael Webb (2017). Are Ideas Getting Harder to Find?. NBER Working Paper 23782.
econ-macro-06-c5.quote: We present a wide range of evidence from various industries, products, and firms showing that research effort is rising substantially while research productivity is declining sharply.
econ-macro-06-c5.claim: Charles Jones's later work showed research productivity is itself falling: we're throwing more researchers at the problem and getting fewer breakthroughs per researcher.
